analysis.one_liner: Suspends federal gas taxes penny-for-penny when gas tops $3.99 and pauses oil company tax breaks during those months.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on April 30, 2026 with 8 Democratic cosponsors and was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: When the national average gasoline price goes above $3.99 a gallon, this bill would cut the federal excise tax on fuel by one cent for every cent the average price exceeds that threshold, so the federal gas tax gradually disappears as prices climb. It would refill the Highway Trust Fund from the general budget so road and tank-cleanup programs don't lose money. During the same high-price months, it would suspend three long-standing tax breaks for oil and gas companies: deductions for intangible drilling costs, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and the marginal well credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, especially commuters and lower-income households who spend a large share of their budget on fuel, would pay less federal tax at the pump whenever gas averages above $3.99. Road construction and underground storage tank cleanup programs would keep their funding because the bill backfills the trust funds from the general budget.

how_it_helps.text: During any month the national average gasoline price exceeds $3.99, the federal fuel excise tax under section 4081 is reduced by 1 cent for each cent the average price exceeds that level.

The Treasury must transfer general-fund money to the Highway Trust Fund and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund equal to the revenue those funds lose from the suspension, so road and cleanup programs are not cut.

During those same high-price months, oil and gas companies lose three tax breaks: intangible drilling cost deductions under section 263(c), the enhanced oil recovery credit under section 43, and the marginal well production credit under section 45I.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which would lose the drilling-cost deduction and two production credits in any month gas averages above $3.99. The general fund — meaning taxpayers and the federal deficit — covers the forgone gas tax revenue, since the bill replaces trust fund money out of general revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and the deficit

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps the Highway Trust Fund whole only by moving money from the general fund, which adds to the deficit whenever the tax is suspended.

Because the trigger is the national average price and the relief arrives through the tax system after fuel is sold, some of the tax savings may end up captured through market pricing rather than fully passed on to drivers — a common criticism of gas-tax holiday proposals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Drivers get real but temporary relief that scales with how high gas prices climb, and the design avoids cutting road and cleanup funding. The tradeoff is honest: the revenue is replaced by deficit spending, and whether the savings reach drivers depends on fuel markets passing them through. Pausing oil industry tax breaks only when prices are high is a narrow pullback, but it gives the bill a pay-for and targets companies at the moment they are earning the most.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced H.R. 8600 in the House on April 30, 2026.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further steps since then.
Eight House members, all Democrats, signed on as cosponsors.
The bill text sets an effective date for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, meaning the tax suspensions would apply retroactively to the current year if enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: oil and gas companies keep their current tax breaks, and drivers have seen no relief, because the bill has not moved out of committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits untouched in committee

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters in the record — the sponsor and eight cosponsors — are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.note: In any month gas averages above $3.99, the bill suspends the intangible drilling cost deduction, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and the marginal well credit — tax breaks the industry otherwise keeps year-round. The suspension is timed to when the industry's prices, and typically its profits, are highest.
The bill backfills the Highway Trust Fund from the general fund, so road construction keeps its funding stream even while the gas tax that normally feeds it is suspended.

industries.industry: Leaking underground storage tank cleanup programs
industries.note: The bill makes the same general-fund backfill for the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund, protecting cleanup funding normally paid for by the fuel tax.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to committee never reach a vote, and this one has sat untouched since its April 30 referral with no Republican support. With a Republican majority controlling the Ways and Means Committee's schedule, it is unlikely to advance before this Congress ends in January 2027.
